newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Hardliners, reformists battle at Bulgaria congress.
newsitem.headline: Hardliners, reformists battle at Bulgaria congress.

text.p: A showdown between hardliners and reformists in Bulgaria's ruling Socialist party entered its final phase on Monday as congress delegates prepared to vote for a new party leader and prime minister.

After Prime Minister Zhan Videnov's surprise resignation on Saturday, Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev led the attack with an outspoken condemnation of the government's failure to halt economic collapse and fight corruption.
But Videnov's supporters fought back, ensuring he was presented again as a candidate for the leadership.
"Videnov's resignation has turned into more and more of a mystery. It's there and it's not there at the same time," Standard daily said in an editorial on Monday.
"The premier said he resigned from all posts but it seems he actually means to strengthen his hold on them."

Delegates voted for a new party supreme council on Monday morning and were expected to elect a party chairman in the afternoon. It was not clear whether the posts of party chief and prime minister would be split.

"While the rest of the world is preparing for a giant party to mark the new century, Bulgaria measures time from congress to plenum, from the first (IMF funding) tranche to suspension of a second tranche, from one lev fixing to a higher one, from one bank failure to the next," said Kapital financial weekly.
The lev has fallen steadily since the beginning of the year and sharply in the last two months as Bulgarians withdrew their savings from illiquid banks to convert them to dollars.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank have suspended funding over Bulgaria's failure to meet reform targets including closing or restructuring loss-making state enterprises and privatising viable firms.
The government is preparing the introduction of a currency board fixed exchange rate regime proposed by the IMF as a last resort to rescue the economy.

Candidates for the party chairmanship were due to be selected after the supreme council. Likely candidates included U.S. born former foreign minister Georgi Pirinski. Delegates said it was not certain that Dobrev would stand against Videnov.

Leading members of the Bulgarian Communist Party renamed themselves Socialists after the end of one-party rule in 1989. The row between hardliners and reformists centres on how far down the road to social democracy they should go.
